title: "The model"
subtitle: "`src/model.ts`: parameters, chamber geometry, and the mechanics of a single cell"
---

This module holds everything about the model that does not depend on the physics engine: every
tunable parameter with its default, the shape of the chamber, and the formulas that turn a cell's
size into a mass, a moment of inertia and a drag. The next chapter, [The simulation](simulation.qmd),
puts these pieces on Rapier.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Where the numbers come from

The model was first written on Box2D, the 2D physics engine behind many games, as a test case in
Box2D's own "testbed" application. Several values below (the cell mass, how friction coefficients
mix, the spring constants of the anchors) are Box2D's own formulas, reproduced here so that the
mechanics stayed the same when the model moved to Rapier. When this site says "the testbed", it
means that original implementation. The [development notes](NOTES.md) record every change since.
:::

The module has five parts:

```{.typescript file=src/model.ts}
<<model-parameters>>

<<model-parameter-type>>

<<model-check-parameters>>

<<model-chamber>>

<<model-cells>>
```

## Parameters

All parameters live in one plain object. Its type is inferred from the object itself, so adding a
parameter is a one-line change, and the command line (`--set name=value`), the browser (URL
parameters) and `Simulation.create()` all accept every parameter by name without further code.

```{.typescript #model-parameters}
export const DEFAULT_PARAMS = {
	<<model-params-stepping>>

	<<model-params-chamber>>

	<<model-params-population>>

	<<model-params-growth>>

	<<model-params-drag>>

	<<model-params-anchors>>

	<<model-params-material>>

	<<model-params-output>>
};
```

Lengths are in model units: a cell is 0.8 units wide, and the chamber is 100 × 60 units. Time is
counted in steps; one step is 1/60 of a simulated second.

### Time stepping and the solver

::: {.parameters}
| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `hertz` | 60 | steps per simulated second; one step lasts 1/`hertz` |
| `substeps` | 1 | Rapier steps per simulation step, each 1/(`hertz` · `substeps`) long |
| `solverIterations` | 8 | iterations of Rapier's contact solver (Rapier's default: 4) |
| `pgsIterations` | 1 | internal iterations per solver iteration (Rapier's default) |
| `contactFrequency` | 720 | contact stiffness, as a natural frequency in Hz; 0 keeps Rapier's default (30) |
| `refreshContacts` | 1 | how a growing cell gets fresh contacts: 1 replace its collider, 2 turn it by π, 0 nothing |
| `rebuildInterval` | 10 000 | with `refreshContacts` = 1, rebuild the Rapier world every this many steps (0 = never) |
:::

Rapier's defaults are made for games, where a pile of boxes may sink into each other a little. A
packed colony of 1700 cells pushing towards the exit is much more demanding: with 4 iterations and
soft (30 Hz) contacts, cells were pressed far into each other once the chamber was full. The solver
settings were found by measuring the overlap between cells over long runs and sweeping iterations
and contact stiffness; stiffer contacts cost nothing per step, extra iterations do. The
[overlap report](reports/overlap-report.md) has the measurements. The last two parameters work
around a Rapier bug that the next chapter explains in
[Growing a collider](simulation.qmd#growing-a-collider).

```{.typescript #model-params-stepping}
hertz: 60,
substeps: 1,
solverIterations: 8,
pgsIterations: 1,
contactFrequency: 720,
refreshContacts: 1,
rebuildInterval: 10000,
```

### The chamber

The chamber spans $x \in [-50, 50]$ and $y \in [140, 200]$. It is closed on the left, right and top
and open at the bottom, where it meets the feeding channel. A cell whose centre leaves this box is
removed: that is how cells exit the chamber.

```{.typescript #model-params-chamber}
minX: -50, maxX: 50,
minY: 140, maxY: 200,
```

### The initial population

A run starts with 1000 cells scattered at random positions and angles. Their initial length is
$\ell_0 = \ell_\text{min} + 0.2\,U\,(\ell_\text{max} - \ell_\text{min})$, with $U$ uniform in
$[0, 1)$, so between 2.4 and 2.88. (The factor 0.2 is the testbed's: only the shortest fifth of the
range is used.) Here and below, a cell's *length* $\ell$ is the distance between the centres of its
two rounded ends; the tip-to-tip length is $\ell + 2r$. Since the cells are placed without regard
for each other, they start out heavily overlapping, and the physics engine needs the first ~3000
steps to push them apart.

```{.typescript #model-params-population}
initialCells: 1000,
minSize: 2.4, maxSize: 4.8,
```

All cell sizes are 0.8 times those of the testbed (whose cells had radius 0.5, initial lengths from
3 to 6, and divided at 6 ± 1.25).

### Growth, division and death

Every cell grows once per *growth cycle* of `growthInterval` = 25 steps, by a factor
$1 + \text{rate}$ in length:

$$
\ell \leftarrow \ell \, (1 + \text{rate}), \qquad \text{rate} = 0.0016 .
$$

A cell therefore doubles its length in $\ln 2 / \ln 1.0016 \approx 433$ growth events, about
10 800 steps. Cells within `wallZone` = 20 units of a side wall grow at `wallRate` instead (the same
value by default, but kept separate so the two regions can be made to differ).

The cells do not all grow on the same step. They are split into `growthGroups` = 5 groups, and the
groups take turns, one every 5 steps; each cell still grows once per cycle. A newborn cell joins its
mother's group. In the testbed every cell grew on the same step, and the whole colony was pushed
outward in one pulse every 25 steps; spreading growth over the cycle removed that visible rhythm.
One group per step (`growthGroups` = 25) would be smoother still, but Rapier pays a fixed cost on
every step in which any collider changes (about 2 ms with a full chamber), so 5 groups is the
compromise. `growthGroups` must divide `growthInterval`.

A cell divides once its length reaches its *reproductive length*, drawn at birth as
$\ell_\text{div} = 4.8 + (U - \tfrac12) \cdot 2$, i.e. uniformly between 3.8 and 5.8. It splits
into two daughters of unequal size: a share $p = 0.3 + 0.2\,U$ of the parent's straight middle
section goes to one daughter and $1 - p$ to the other.

```{.typescript #model-params-growth}
growthInterval: 25,
growthGroups: 5,
rate: 0.002 * 0.8,
wallRate: 0.002 * 0.8,
wallZone: 20,
reproductionProportionMin: 0.3,
reproductionProportionRange: 0.2,
reproductiveLengthMean: 4.8,
reproductiveLengthSpread: 2.0,
centredDivision: 1,
randomDeathProbability: 0.001 * 0.15,
```

`centredDivision` = 1 places the two daughters so that together they fill exactly the parent's
outline. The testbed (`centredDivision` = 0) shifted both daughters along the axis, so that the tip
of one of them poked up to 10% of the cell width past the parent's end, into whichever neighbour
touched it there. The [division code](simulation.qmd#division) shows both placements.

Finally, at each growth event a cell dies with probability `randomDeathProbability`
($1.5 \times 10^{-4}$) and is removed.

### Drag

Bacteria live where viscosity dominates: they stop as soon as nothing pushes them. A physics
engine, in contrast, conserves momentum, and without drag the colony would stream out of the
chamber. The model therefore damps every cell's velocity and spin.

::: {.parameters}
| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `airResistance` | 0.007 · 0.8² | linear drag coefficient $k$ (force = $-k\,v$) |
| `angularAirResistance` | 0.007 · 0.8⁴ | the same for rotation |
| `continuousDrag` | 1 | 1: drag acts every step, as body damping; 0: the testbed's kick on growth steps |
| `dragClamp` | 1 | with `continuousDrag` = 0, a kick removes at most all of a cell's velocity |
:::

```{.typescript #model-params-drag}
airResistance: 0.007 * 0.8 ** 2,
angularAirResistance: 0.007 * 0.8 ** 4,
continuousDrag: 1,
dragClamp: 1,
```

The coefficients are the testbed's (0.007), scaled with the cell size so that drag still removes
the same *fraction* of a cell's velocity: mass scales with area ($0.8^2$) and the moment of inertia
with mass times length squared ($0.8^4$).

The testbed applied drag as a single kick on growth steps. Each kick removed 50–100% of a cell's
velocity at once and nothing slowed the cells in between, so the colony moved in a stop-and-go
rhythm. With `continuousDrag` = 1 the same average drag is applied smoothly, by the physics engine,
on every step; the [formulas](#drag-formulas) are below. `dragClamp` only matters for the old
kick: for cells shorter than about 1.4, a kick removed *more* than all of their spin, reversing it
and amplifying it, so small isolated cells spun up like propellers. The clamp caps the kick at
stopping the cell.

### Anchoring to the surface

Cells near the side walls can attach to the chamber floor, as bacteria do with extracellular
matrix. In the model an *anchor* is a zero-length spring between the cell's centre and a fixed
point where the cell was when it attached.

::: {.parameters}
| Parameter | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `anchorProbability` | 0.001 | chance per growth event that a cell in a wall zone attaches |
| `anchorFrequencyHz` | 0.8 | natural frequency of the spring |
| `anchorDampingRatio` | 0.3 | damping ratio of the spring |
| `anchorLifetimeSteps` | 12 000 | the anchor is removed after this many steps |
| `anchorMaxStretch` | 4 | the anchor lets go when its cell is farther than this from the anchor point (0 = never) |
:::

```{.typescript #model-params-anchors}
anchorProbability: 0.001,
anchorFrequencyHz: 0.8,
anchorDampingRatio: 0.3,
anchorLifetimeSteps: 12000,
anchorMaxStretch: 4,
```

The testbed removed anchors after 200 seconds of *wall-clock* time; 12 000 steps is 200 s at 60
steps per second. Its anchors also never let go otherwise. The 0.8 Hz springs are too soft to hold
a cell against a packed colony, so once the chamber was full the colony dragged anchored cells
several units away, and the stretched springs pulled them back hard enough to push them into their
neighbours. Letting go beyond a maximum stretch, like matrix that yields under strain, removed
those deep overlaps in the validation runs, which used a limit of 2 units; the default is now 4
units, five cell widths.

### Cell shape and material

A cell is a *capsule*: a rectangle with a half disc at each end, `radius` = 0.4 (so the cell is
0.8 wide). Collisions are perfectly inelastic (`restitution` = 0). Each cell gets its own friction
coefficient, uniform in $[0, 1)$, when it is born; it is not a parameter.

```{.typescript #model-params-material}
radius: 0.4,
density: 0.0001,
restitution: 0.0,
```

### Output

The positions of all cells are recorded every `snapshotInterval` steps
([Randomness and records](recording.qmd) describes the format).

```{.typescript #model-params-output}
snapshotInterval: 300,
```

### The parameter type

A run is described by the parameters plus a random seed. The type is derived from the defaults,
so it can never fall out of step with them.

```{.typescript #model-parameter-type}
export type SimulationParams = typeof DEFAULT_PARAMS & { seed: number };
```

### Checking parameters

Most parameters accept any number, but four are counts that the stepping logic relies on, so they
are checked when a simulation is created, and a bad value stops it with a clear message:

- `growthInterval` and `growthGroups` must be positive integers, and the groups must divide the
  cycle evenly; otherwise some groups would never get a turn to grow.
- `snapshotInterval` must be a multiple of `growthInterval`, so that every snapshot is taken at the
  same point of the growth cycle. (In the testbed, which only looked for snapshots on growth steps,
  other values silently skipped snapshots.)
- `substeps` must be a positive integer.

```{.typescript #model-check-parameters}
export function checkParams(p: SimulationParams): void {
	if (!Number.isInteger(p.growthInterval) || p.growthInterval < 1) {
		throw new Error(`growthInterval must be a positive integer (got ${p.growthInterval})`);
	}
	if (!Number.isInteger(p.snapshotInterval) || p.snapshotInterval < 1 || p.snapshotInterval % p.growthInterval !== 0) {
		throw new Error(`snapshotInterval must be a positive multiple of growthInterval (${p.growthInterval}); got ${p.snapshotInterval}`);
	}
	if (!Number.isInteger(p.growthGroups) || p.growthGroups < 1 || p.growthInterval % p.growthGroups !== 0) {
		throw new Error(`growthGroups must be a positive integer that divides growthInterval (${p.growthInterval}); got ${p.growthGroups}`);
	}
	if (!Number.isInteger(p.substeps) || p.substeps < 1) {
		throw new Error(`substeps must be a positive integer (got ${p.substeps})`);
	}
}
```

## The chamber geometry

The chamber is described as data, so that the physics ([walls](simulation.qmd#the-chamber-walls)),
the overlap check and the drawing all use the same shapes:

- three straight walls: the top wall, and the two side walls, open at the bottom;
- rows of small triangles along the walls, each sticking one unit into the chamber: 12 on each side
  wall, every 5 units, and 20 along the top.

```{.typescript #model-chamber}
<<model-geometry-types>>

<<model-triangle-rows>>

<<model-wall-triangles>>

<<model-chamber-data>>
```

A point is a plain pair of coordinates. A triangle is stored as three vertices plus an offset, the
way the testbed created them: one triangle shape, repeated at regular offsets.

```{.typescript #model-geometry-types}
export interface Point { x: number; y: number; }

export interface Triangle { offset: Point; vertices: [Point, Point, Point]; }
```

`triangleRows` repeats one or more triangle shapes `count` times, shifting the $i$-th copy by
$i \cdot \text{step}$:

```{.typescript #model-triangle-rows}
function triangleRows(count: number, step: Point, ...vertexSets: [Point, Point, Point][]): Triangle[] {
	const rows: Triangle[] = [];
	for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
		for (const vertices of vertexSets) { rows.push({ offset: { x: i * step.x, y: i * step.y }, vertices }); }
	}
	return rows;
}
```

The three triangle shapes sit at the bottom of each side wall and at the left end of the top wall.
Each has two vertices on the wall and a third one unit inside the chamber.

```{.typescript #model-wall-triangles}
const RIGHT_WALL_TRIANGLE: [Point, Point, Point] = [{ x: 50, y: 140 }, { x: 50, y: 142 }, { x: 49, y: 141 }];
const LEFT_WALL_TRIANGLE: [Point, Point, Point] = [{ x: -50, y: 140 }, { x: -50, y: 142 }, { x: -49, y: 141 }];
const TOP_WALL_TRIANGLE: [Point, Point, Point] = [{ x: -50, y: 200 }, { x: -48, y: 200 }, { x: -49, y: 199 }];
```

The chamber lists the triangles first and then the walls, in the order the testbed created them,
together with the walls' friction coefficient (Box2D's default, 0.2).

```{.typescript #model-chamber-data}
export const CHAMBER = {
	triangles: [
		...triangleRows(12, { x: 0, y: 5 }, RIGHT_WALL_TRIANGLE, LEFT_WALL_TRIANGLE),
		...triangleRows(20, { x: 5, y: 0 }, TOP_WALL_TRIANGLE),
	],
	edges: [
		[{ x: -50, y: 200 }, { x: 50, y: 200 }],
		[{ x: 50, y: 200 }, { x: 50, y: 140 }],
		[{ x: -50, y: 200 }, { x: -50, y: 140 }],
	] as [Point, Point][],
	friction: 0.2,
};
```

## Cells

The rest of the module is about individual cells: their colours, and the formulas for drag and
mass.

```{.typescript #model-cells}
<<model-colours>>

<<model-drag>>

<<model-mass>>

<<model-orientation>>
```

### Colours

Cells are coloured by where they are: dark grey when they are first placed, green in the wall
zones and magenta in the centre. The colour is part of the cell's state: it is updated on growth
steps, when the cell's region is checked, and daughters inherit it. The drawing code uses it to
tell the regions apart.

```{.typescript #model-colours}
export interface RGB { r: number; g: number; b: number; }
export const COLOR_INITIAL: RGB = { r: 0.3, g: 0.35, b: 0.3 };
export const COLOR_WALL: RGB = { r: 0.1, g: 0.8, b: 0.18 };
export const COLOR_CENTRE: RGB = { r: 0.8, g: 0.1, b: 0.6 };
```

### Drag formulas {#drag-formulas}

In the testbed a cell was a Box2D body made of three *fixtures*: a box and two discs. Drag was a
force $-k\,v$ applied to each fixture, so three times per cell, during one step $\Delta t$ every
growth cycle.

```{.typescript #model-drag}
export const DRAG_APPLICATIONS_PER_CELL = 3;

<<model-drag-fraction>>

<<model-damping-rate>>
```

**The kick.** One kick changes the velocity by $\Delta v = -3 k v \, \Delta t / m$, so it removes
the fraction

$$
f = \frac{3\,k\,\Delta t}{m}
$$

of the velocity (and likewise of the spin, with the moment of inertia $I$ in place of $m$). For a
very small cell $f$ can exceed 1, which reverses the motion; with the clamp, $f$ is at most 1.

```{.typescript #model-drag-fraction}
export function dragFraction(coefficient: number, massOrInertia: number, dt: number, clamp: boolean): number {
	const fraction = DRAG_APPLICATIONS_PER_CELL * coefficient * dt / massOrInertia;
	return clamp && fraction > 1 ? 1 : fraction;
}
```

**Continuous drag.** The kick delivers an impulse $3 k v \,\Delta t$ once every `growthInterval`
($G$) steps. Spread evenly over those $G$ steps, that is a force of $3 k v / G$, i.e. a damping
rate

$$
\gamma = \frac{3\,k}{G\,m} \quad [\text{s}^{-1}] .
$$

Rapier, like Box2D, applies a body's damping rate every step as
$v \leftarrow v / (1 + \Delta t\,\gamma)$. Since a cell's mass never changes (see below), the rate
is set once when the cell is born and costs nothing per step.

```{.typescript #model-damping-rate}
export function continuousDampingRate(coefficient: number, massOrInertia: number, growthInterval: number): number {
	return DRAG_APPLICATIONS_PER_CELL * coefficient / (growthInterval * massOrInertia);
}
```

### Mass and moment of inertia

The mass and moment of inertia are computed exactly as Box2D computed them for the testbed's cell:
a box of half-widths $a = r$ and $b = \ell/2$, plus a full disc of radius $a$ at each end. The half
discs that overlap the box are counted twice, as Box2D did. With density $\rho$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_\text{box} &= 4 \rho a b, & I_\text{box} &= m_\text{box} \frac{(2a)^2 + (2b)^2}{12}, \\
m_\text{cap} &= \rho \pi a^2, & I_\text{cap} &= m_\text{cap} \left(\tfrac12 a^2 + b^2\right), \\
m &= m_\text{box} + 2 m_\text{cap}, & I &= I_\text{box} + 2 I_\text{cap},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $I_\text{cap}$ is a disc's own moment plus the parallel-axis term for its distance $b$ from
the centre. Box2D computed these once, when a cell was created, and never again as the cell grew.
The model keeps that: a cell's mass is fixed at birth.

```{.typescript #model-mass}
export function cellMassProperties(length: number, radius: number, density: number): { mass: number, inertia: number } {
	const a = radius, b = length / 2;
	const boxMass = density * 4 * a * b;
	const capMass = density * Math.PI * a * a;
	const boxInertia = boxMass * ((2 * a) ** 2 + (2 * b) ** 2) / 12;
	const capInertia = capMass * (0.5 * a * a + b * b);
	return { mass: boxMass + 2 * capMass, inertia: boxInertia + 2 * capInertia };
}
```

### Orientation

The recorded orientation of a cell is its angle as a fraction of $\pi$, folded into $[0, 1]$: a rod
looks the same when turned by half a turn, so angles $\theta$ and $\theta + \pi$ are the same
orientation. An orientation of 0 means the cell lies along the $y$ axis, pointing at the exit.

```{.typescript #model-orientation}
export function orientationOf(angle: number): number {
	return angle > 0 ? (angle / Math.PI) % 1 : 1 + (angle / Math.PI) % 1;
}
```
